title: Iraq's Oil Crackdown Sparks New Showdown With Kurdistan | OilPrice.com

Iraq’s federal government is using its oil-smuggling case against the pro-Iranian militia Kata’ib Hezbollah south of Baghdad to force the Kurdistan Regional Government in the north to hand over more oil and open its fields to federal inspectors.

South of Baghdad, the Iraqi PM has ordered federal forces to take over a pipeline at Jurf al-Sakhar (Babil province) that the pro-Iranian militia has been illegally tapping into since at least 2021. Iraq’s federal government is using its oil-smuggling case against the pro-Iranian militia Kata’ib Hezbollah south of Baghdad to force the Kurdistan Regional Government in the north to hand over more oil and open its fields to federal inspectors.

South of Baghdad, the Iraqi PM has ordered federal forces to take over a pipeline at Jurf al-Sakhar (Babil province) that the pro-Iranian militia has been illegally tapping into since at least 2021. Iraqi officials estimate the group made away with hundreds of millions of dollars in crude. Baghdad gave Kata’ib Hezbollah until Friday to leave, and by midweek the militia had dug trenches and handed out anti-armour weapons around the town. The standoff split the Coordination Framework, Iraq’s ruling Shia alliance, which refused to back an assault, and drew Iran’s Quds Force commander, Esmail Qaani, to Baghdad.

Late Thursday, Baghdad announced a compromise, and on Friday morning federal forces began setting up a joint command headquarters in Jurf to run an army brigade, a federal police brigade, an Energy Police regiment assigned to guard the pipeline and two brigades of the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF, the state-funded umbrella of mostly Shia armed groups that includes Kata’ib Hezbollah itself). The PMF says its brigades are replacing Kata’ib Hezbollah’s, though some of the militia’s fighters will serve in the new units. Zaidi’s office says the militia will withdraw. Kata’ib Hezbollah says it will neither leave nor hand over its weapons, and wants any handover delayed until June 30 next year.

In the north, Baghdad is now trying to use the same playbook on Erbil, accusing the KRG of smuggling by way of giving Baghdad less than it’s producing. Zaidi’s spokesman has said the Iraqi army could enter the Kurdistan Region to pursue smugglers. The draft 2027 Iraqi federal budget requires the KRG to deliver 400,000 bpd to the country’s federal oil marketer, SOMO, against the roughly 255,000 the KRG says it produces. Baghdad then ties the salaries of Kurdish public employees to those deliveries; so, less crude means a hole in KRG funding for public salaries (that’s patronage it needs to maintain power).

Baghdad has opened several smuggling probes that reach into the KRG. Zaidi has promised to root out smuggling from Zakho, the border town where the Kurds hand their crude to SOMO, to Basra. A parliamentary committee is examining crude moved from Kirkuk and the KRG through Iran to Afghanistan, and the federal Integrity Commission has a team on the ground at the oilfields between Kirkuk and the Region.

The two sides disagree on how much oil the KRG produces. The KRG offers Baghdad 250,000 to 280,000 bpd and cites a Wood Mackenzie estimate of about 255,000. But Baghdad says its intelligence shows the KRG is producing more than 400,000, with an adviser to Zaidi even floating 650,000 (which is highly unlikely). The federal Oil Ministry has proposed stationing SOMO staff at Kurdish oilfields to verify output, and Baghdad’s directly calling this “smuggling”. What this accusation is intended to do is force Erbil to prove Baghdad wrong by opening its fields and meters to federal inspectors.

The KRG is negotiating from its weakest position in years. A drone strike shut the Khor Mor gas field on Nov. 8 and took 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts off the Kurdish grid. Supply has recovered only to about 1,500 megawatts, and KRG PM Masrour Barzani says a restart depends on repairs and security guarantees. Khor Mor has been attacked 12 times since the start of 2025.

Jurf is now the litmus test. If the joint command takes control and federal Energy Police hold the pipeline, Zaidi will have the arrangement he wants and will press the KRG for the same at its oilfields and the Zakho metering point. If Kata’ib Hezbollah refuses to leave, the federal forces in Jurf will be sharing ground with a militia on the state payroll that says it is keeping its weapons, and the Shia alliance that keeps Zaidi in office will be back where it was on Monday.
